p: (1) The President, or the Governor or Rajpramukh of a State, shall not be answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his office or for any act done or purporting to be done by him in the exercise and performance of those powers and duties:

Provided that the conduct of the President may be brought under review by any court, tribunal or body appointed or designated by either House of Parliament for the investigation of a charge under article 61:
Provided further that nothing in this clause shall be construed as restricting the right of any person to bring appropriate proceedings against the Government of India or the Government of a State.
(2) No criminal proceedings whatsoever shall be instituted or continued against the President, or the Governor {1}*** of a State, in any court during his term of office.
(3) No process for the arrest or imprisonment of the President, or the Governor {1}*** of a State, shall issue from any court during his term of office.

(4) No civil proceedings in which relief is claimed against the President, or the Governor {1}*** of a State, shall be instituted during his term of office in any court in respect of any act done or purporting to be done by him in his personal capacity, whether before or after he entered upon his office as President, or as Governor {1}*** of such State, until the expiration of two months next after notice in writing has been delivered to the President or the Governor {1}***, as the case may be, or left at his office stating the nature of the proceedings, the cause of action therefor, the name, description and place of residence of the party by whom such proceedings are to be instituted and the relief which he claims.
f: The words "or Rajpramukh" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
361.s: The President and Governors do not answer to any court for acts done in office, though people can still sue the Government and a body chosen by Parliament can review the President's conduct on an impeachment charge. During their term, no criminal case or arrest order is allowed, and civil cases over personal acts need two months' written notice.

p: (1) No person shall be liable to any proceedings, civil or criminal, in any court in respect of the publication in a newspaper of a substantially true report of any proceedings of either House of Parliament or the Legislative Assembly, or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature, of a State, unless the publication is proved to have been made with malice:

Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to the publication of any report of the proceedings of a secret sitting of either House of Parliament or the Legislative Assembly, or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature, of a State.

(2) Clause (1) shall apply in relation to reports or matters broadcast by means of wireless telegraphy as part of any programme or service provided by means of a broadcasting station as it applies in relation to reports or matters published in a newspaper.
Explanation.—In this article, “newspaper” includes a news agency report containing material for publication in a newspaper.]
f: Art. 361A ins. by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 42 (w.e.f. 20-6-1979).
361A.s: No one can be sued or prosecuted for publishing a substantially true newspaper report of proceedings of Parliament or a State Legislature, unless it was done with malice. The same protection covers broadcast reports and news agency reports, but not reports of secret sittings.

p: A member of a House belonging to any political party who is disqualified for being a member of the House under paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule shall also be disqualified to hold any remunerative political post for duration of the period commencing from the date of his disqualification till the date on which the term of his office as such member would expire or till the date on which he contests an election to a House and is declared elected, whichever is earlier.
Explanation.— For the purposes of this article,—
(a) the expression “House” has the meaning assigned to it in clause (a) of paragraph 1 of the Tenth Schedule;
(b) the expression “remunerative political post” means any office—

(i) under the Government of India or the Government of a State where the salary or remuneration for such office is paid out of the public revenue of the Government of India or the Government of the State, as the case may be; or

(ii) under a body, whether incorporated or not, which is wholly or partially owned by the Government of India or the Government of State, and the salary or remuneration for such office is paid by such body,
except where such salary or remuneration paid is compensatory in nature.]
f: Art. 361B ins. by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act, 2003, s. 4 (w.e.f. 1-1-2004).
361B.s: A party member of a legislature who is disqualified under paragraph 2 of the Tenth Schedule cannot hold any paid political post until their term would have ended or until they are elected again, whichever comes first. A paid political post is a government office, or one in a government-owned body, unless the pay is only compensatory.

362.st: Omitted by the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, s. 2 (w.e.f. 28-12-1971).

p: (1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution but subject to the provisions of article 143, neither the Supreme Court nor any other court shall have jurisdiction in any dispute arising out of any provision of a treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument which was entered into or executed before the commencement of this Constitution by any Ruler of an Indian State and to which the Government of the Dominion of India or any of its predecessor Governments was a party and which has or has been continued in operation after such commencement, or in any dispute in respect of any right accruing under or any liability or obligation arising out of any of the provisions of this Constitution relating to any such treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument.
(2) In this article—
(a) “Indian State” means any territory recognised before the commencement of this Constitution by His Majesty or the Government of the Dominion of India as being such a State; and
(b) “Ruler” includes the Prince, Chief or other person recognised before such commencement by His Majesty or the Government of the Dominion of India as the Ruler of any Indian State.
363.s: Except as allowed under article 143, no court, including the Supreme Court, can hear disputes arising from treaties, agreements, sanads or similar documents made before the Constitution between a Ruler of an Indian State and the Government of the Dominion of India or its predecessors.

p: Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution or in any law for the time being in force—

(a) the Prince, Chief or other person who, at any time before the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, was recognised by the President as the Ruler of an Indian State or any person who, at any time before such commencement, was recognised by the President as the successor of such ruler shall, on and from such commencement, cease to be recognised as such Ruler or the successor of such Ruler;

(b) on and from the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, privy purse is abolished and all rights, liabilities and obligations in respect of privy purse are extinguished and accordingly the Ruler or, as the case may be, the successor of such Ruler, referred to in clause (a) or any other person shall not be paid any sum as privy purse.]
f: Art. 363A ins. by the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, s. 3 (w.e.f. 28-12-1971).
363A.s: From the Twenty-sixth Amendment of 1971, no one is recognised any longer as the Ruler of an Indian State or a Ruler's successor. Privy purses are abolished, all related rights and duties end, and no one is to be paid any privy purse.

p: (1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by public notification direct that as from such date as may be specified in the notification—

(a) any law made by Parliament or by the Legislature of a State shall not apply to any major port or aerodrome or shall apply thereto subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the notification; or

(b) any existing law shall cease to have effect in any major port or aerodrome except as respects things done or omitted to be done before the said date, or shall in its application to such port or aerodrome have effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the notification.
(2) In this article—
(a) “major port” means a port declared to be a major port by or under any law made by Parliament or any existing law and includes all areas for the time being included within the limits of such port;
(b) “aerodrome” means aerodrome as defined for the purposes of the enactments relating to airways, aircraft and air navigation.
364.s: The President can, by public notification, direct that a law of Parliament or of a State, or an existing law, does not apply to a major port or aerodrome from a set date, or applies there only with specified exceptions or changes.

p: Where any State has failed to comply with, or to give effect to, any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union under any of the provisions of this Constitution, it shall be lawful for the President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
365.s: If a State fails to follow or carry out directions given by the Union under the Constitution, the President may treat this as a situation where the State Government cannot be carried on according to the Constitution.
k: state government cannot be carried on

p: In this Constitution, unless the context otherwise requires, the following expressions have the meanings hereby respectively assigned to them, that is to say—
(1) “agricultural income” means agricultural income as defined for the purposes of the enactments relating to Indian income-tax;

(2) “an Anglo-Indian” means a person whose father or any of whose other male progenitors in the male line is or was of European descent but who is domiciled within the territory of India and is or was born within such territory of parents habitually resident therein and not established there for temporary purposes only;
(3) “article” means an article of this Constitution;
(4) “borrow” includes the raising of money by the grant of annuities, and “loan” shall be construed accordingly;
(5) “clause” means a clause of the article in which the expression occurs;
(6) “corporation tax” means any tax on income, so far as that tax is payable by companies and is a tax in the case of which the following conditions are fulfilled:—
(a) that it is not chargeable in respect of agricultural income;
(b) that no deduction in respect of the tax paid by companies is, by any enactments which may apply to the tax, authorised to be made from dividends payable by the companies to individuals;

(c) that no provision exists for taking the tax so paid into account in computing for the purposes of Indian income-tax the total income of individuals receiving such dividends, or in computing the Indian income-tax payable by, or refundable to, such individuals;

(7) “corresponding Province”, “corresponding Indian State” or “corresponding State” means in cases of doubt such Province, Indian State or State as may be determined by the President to be the corresponding Province, the corresponding Indian State or the corresponding State, as the case may be, for the particular purpose in question;
(8) “debt” includes any liability in respect of any obligation to repay capital sums by way of annuities and any liability under any guarantee, and “debt charges” shall be construed accordingly;

(9) “estate duty” means a duty to be assessed on or by reference to the principal value, ascertained in accordance with such rules as may be prescribed by or under laws made by Parliament or the Legislature of a State relating to the duty, of all property passing upon death or deemed, under the provisions of the said laws, so to pass;

(10) “existing law” means any law, Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule or regulation passed or made before the commencement of this Constitution by any Legislature, authority or person having power to make such a law, Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule or regulation;
(11) “Federal Court” means the Federal Court constituted under the Government of India Act, 1935;
(12) “goods” includes all materials, commodities, and articles;
{2}[(12A) “goods and services tax” means any tax on supply of goods, or services or both except taxes on the supply of the alcoholic liquor for human consumption];
(13) “guarantee” includes any obligation undertaken before the commencement of this Constitution to make payments in the event of the profits of an undertaking falling short of a specified amount;
(14) “High Court” means any Court which is deemed for the purposes of this Constitution to be a High Court for any State and includes—
(a) any Court in the territory of India constituted or reconstituted under this Constitution as a High Court; and
(b) any other Court in the territory of India which may be declared by Parliament by law to be a High Court for all or any of the purposes of this Constitution;
(15) “Indian State” means any territory which the Government of the Dominion of India recognised as such a State;
(16) “Part” means a Part of this Constitution;

(17) “pension” means a pension, whether contributory or not, of any kind whatsoever payable to or in respect of any person, and includes retired pay so payable; a gratuity so payable and any sum or sums so payable by way of the return, with or without interest thereon or any other addition thereto, of subscriptions to a provident fund;
(18) “Proclamation of Emergency” means a Proclamation issued under clause (1) of article 352;
(19) “public notification” means a notification in the Gazette of India, or, as the case may be, the Official Gazette of a State;
(20) “railway” does not include—
(a) a tramway wholly within a municipal area; or
(b) any other line of communication wholly situate in one State and declared by Parliament by law not to be a railway;

{4}[(22) “Ruler” means the Prince, Chief or other person who, at any time before the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, was recognised by the President as the Ruler of an Indian State or any person who, at any time before such commencement, was recognised by the President as the successor of such Ruler;]
(23) “Schedule” means a Schedule to this Constitution;

(24) “Scheduled Castes” means such castes, races or tribes or parts of or groups within such castes, races or tribes as are deemed under article 341 to be Scheduled Castes for the purposes of this Constitution;

(25) “Scheduled Tribes” means such tribes or tribal communities or parts of or groups within such tribes or tribal communities as are deemed under article 342 to be Scheduled Tribes for the purposes of this Constitution;
(26) “securities” includes stock;
{6}[(26A) “Services” means anything other than goods;
(26B) “State” with reference to articles 246A, 268, 269, 269A and article 279A includes a Union territory with Legislature];

{7}[(26C) "socially and educationally backward classes" means such backward classes as are so deemed under article 342A for the purposes of the Central Government or the State or Union territory, as the case may be];
(27) “sub-clause” means a sub-clause of the clause in which the expression occurs;
(28) “taxation” includes the imposition of any tax or impost, whether general or local or special, and “tax” shall be construed accordingly;
(29) “tax on income” includes a tax in the nature of an excess profits tax;
{8}[(29A) “tax on the sale or purchase of goods” includes—
(a) a tax on the transfer, otherwise than in pursuance of a contract, of property in any goods for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration;
(b) a tax on the transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of a works contract;
(c) a tax on the delivery of goods on hire-purchase or any system of payment by instalments;
(d) a tax on the transfer of the right to use any goods for any purpose (whether or not for a specified period) for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration;
(e) a tax on the supply of goods by any unincorporated association or body of persons to a member thereof for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration;

(f) a tax on the supply, by way of or as part of any service or in any other manner whatsoever, of goods, being food or any other article for human consumption or any drink (whether or not intoxicating), where such supply or service, is for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration,
and such transfer, delivery or supply of any goods shall be deemed to be
a sale of those goods by the person making the transfer, delivery or
supply and a purchase of those goods by the person to whom such
transfer, delivery or supply is made;]
{9}[(30) "Union territory" means any Union territory specified in the First Schedule and includes any other territory comprised within the territory of India but not specified in that Schedule.]
f: Cl. (4A) was ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 54 (w.e.f. 1-2-1977) and subsequently omitted by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977, s. 11 (w.e.f. 13-4-1978).
Ins. by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, s. 14(i) (w.e.f. 16-9-2016).
Cl. (21) omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
Subs. by the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, s. 4 (w.e.f. 28-12-1971).

Cl. (26A) was ins. by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, s. 54 (w.e.f. 1-2-1977), and subsequently omitted by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment) Act, 1977, s. 11 (w.e.f. 13-4-1978).
Ins. by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, s. 14(ii) (w.e.f. 16-9-2016).

Cl. (26C) was ins. by the Constitution (One Hundred and second Amendment) Act, 2018, s. 5 (w.e.f. 14-8-2018), and subsequently subs. by the Constitution (One Hundred and Fifth Amendment) Act, 2021, s. 4 (w.e.f. 15-9-2021).
Cl. (29A) ins. by the Constitution (Forty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1982, s. 4 (w.e.f. 2-2-1983).
Subs. by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. for cl. (30) (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
366.s: Gives the meaning of key words used throughout the Constitution, such as agricultural income, Anglo-Indian, existing law, goods, services, goods and services tax, High Court, pension, Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Union territory and tax on the sale or purchase of goods. These meanings apply unless the context requires otherwise.
k: meaning of goods and services tax

p: (1) Unless the context otherwise requires, the General Clauses Act, 1897, shall, subject to any adaptations and modifications that may be made therein under article 372, apply for the interpretation of this Constitution as it applies for the interpretation of an Act of the Legislature of the Dominion of India.

(2) Any reference in this Constitution to Acts or laws of, or made by, Parliament, or to Acts or laws of, or made by, the Legislature of a State {1}***, shall be construed as including a reference to an Ordinance made by the President or, to an Ordinance made by a Governor {2}***, as the case may be.
(3) For the purposes of this Constitution “foreign State” means any State other than India:
Provided that, subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament, the President may by order{3} declare any State not to be a foreign State for such purposes as may be specified in the order.
f: The words and letters "specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule" omitted by s. 29 and Sch., ibid. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
The words "or Rajpramukh" omitted by s. 29 and Sch., ibid. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
See the Constitution (Declaration as to Foreign States) Order, 1950 (C.O. 2).
Added by the Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019 (C.O. 272) (w.e.f. 5-8-2019).
367.s: The General Clauses Act, 1897 guides how the Constitution is read, and laws of Parliament or a State Legislature include Ordinances of the President or a Governor. A foreign State is any State other than India, unless the President declares otherwise for certain purposes.
fh: specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule
Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 2019

why: Minerva Mills (1980) held that abrogating Articles 14 and 19 for a class of laws destroys the basic structure; Coelho (2007) treats the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21 as the test for Ninth Schedule laws.
Coelho (2007) called Article 32 "an important and integral part of the basic structure", and L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that judicial review under it cannot be ousted.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that the High Courts' power of judicial review under Article 226, and their superintendence under Article 227, are part of the inviolable basic structure.
Minerva Mills (1980) held that a limited amending power is itself a basic feature, so Parliament cannot amend this article to make its power unlimited.

The NJAC case (2015) struck down the Ninety-ninth Amendment's new method of appointing judges as a breach of judicial independence, so the core of how judges are appointed is part of the basic structure.
Names India as a Union of States. Abolishing the Union or the States would undo federalism and India's sovereignty, both part of the framework.
This is the hook for testing laws against fundamental rights. Courts have said the power to test legislation "can never be ousted".
Core guarantees against discrimination and untouchability. Coelho (2007) named Article 15 among the rights forming part of the basic structure.
Freedom of religion is the main textual home of secularism, which the Court has repeatedly called a basic feature.
Judicial review by the High Courts, held to be basic, depends on the High Courts existing.
Adult suffrage is the foundation of democracy and free and fair elections.
Kesavananda Bharati (Khanna J) held that the part of the Preamble relating to the basic structure cannot be amended; Balram Singh (2024) upheld adding "socialist" and "secular".
Defines "the State" against which fundamental rights are enforced; gutting it would hollow out the rights.
Equality of opportunity in public employment is part of the equality code, though clauses on reservation have been changed and upheld.
Basic protections of personal liberty and fair criminal process, closely tied to Article 21.
Bans on forced labour and child labour in hazardous work relate to human dignity; no case has tested their repeal.
Religious freedom of groups and the bar on State religious instruction carry secularism into practice.
Minority rights to culture and to run educational institutions support pluralism and secularism.
The Directive to separate the judiciary from the executive expresses separation of powers and judicial independence.
An elected President as head of state is part of the republican form of government.
How the President is elected. Entrenched: changing it needs ratification by half the States.
Extent of Union executive power, one half of the federal balance. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
Ministers advise the President and answer collectively to the Lok Sabha: the core of parliamentary government.
An elected Parliament, with the States represented in it. Representation of the States is entrenched.
Fixed terms for the Houses guarantee periodic elections.
Parliament cannot discuss a judge's conduct except on a motion for removal, a rule tied to judicial independence.
Judges' salaries cannot be cut to their disadvantage while in office, a guard on judicial independence.
Courts of record with power to punish contempt, part of the courts' ability to make their orders effective.
The Supreme Court settles disputes between the Union and the States, a federal safeguard.
Special leave to appeal lets the Supreme Court correct any court or tribunal, central to access to justice.
Each State has its own executive, part of the federal structure.
Extent of State executive power. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
State ministers advise the Governor and answer to the Assembly: parliamentary government at State level.
An elected State Legislature with fixed terms, needed for both democracy and federalism.
Transfers of High Court judges. The NJAC case struck down the 2014 change to this article as part of the same scheme.
High Court control over the subordinate courts keeps the district judiciary independent of the executive.
The division of law-making power between Parliament and the States. Entrenched under Article 368(2).
No tax without the authority of law, a basic rule-of-law guarantee.
An independent Election Commission conducts elections; without it free and fair elections would be at risk.
A single electoral roll with no exclusion on grounds of religion, race, caste or sex.
The right to education. Its insertion was upheld, but no case says whether removing it would breach the basic structure.
The welfare-state directives most closely tied to the balance between Parts III and IV. Removing them might upset that balance; untested.
Courts cannot question the validity of legislative proceedings on grounds of procedure. Touches both separation of powers and judicial review.
Binding precedent and the power to do complete justice. Important to the Court's role, but not tested as basic.
An independent auditor of public accounts supports the rule of law and accountability; untested.
Organisational rules for the High Courts. Some core is needed for judicial review, but the details can change.
President's Rule. Its use is reviewable (Bommai), and abuse can damage federalism and democracy, but the article itself is not part of the basic structure.
Suspension of rights during emergency. Since 1978, Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended; widening this power again could touch the essence of rights.
Parliament already changes State boundaries by ordinary law; the federal structure survives individual changes.
Citizenship rules. Parliament already controls citizenship by law under Article 11.
These shield certain laws from fundamental rights challenges. Removing them would restore rights, not damage the structure.
Powers to adapt or restrict rights for armed forces and martial law; administrative in nature.
Individual Directive Principles. The balance between Parts III and IV is basic, but no single directive has been held essential.
Fundamental duties were added in 1976 and are not enforceable in court.
Detailed rules on the President, Vice-President and conduct of business. Can change without touching a basic feature.
Detailed rules on Parliament's membership, officers and procedure.
Legislative and financial procedure, and ordinances. Can be redesigned without damaging democracy itself.
Organisation and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court beyond its core review power. Many have been amended before.
Form and reporting of public accounts.
Detailed rules on Governors and State executive business.
Detailed rules on State Legislatures, their officers and members.
State legislative and financial procedure, assent to Bills and ordinances.
Detailed rules on High Court judges and jurisdiction beyond the core review power.
Appointment and rules for district judges and subordinate courts.
How Union territories are governed. Parliament has changed this often.
Panchayats, added in 1992. Local democracy, but not part of the original framework or any holding.
Administration of Scheduled and Tribal Areas.
Specific rules within the division of legislative power. Entrenched where in Chapter I of Part XI, but individually changeable.
Administrative relations between the Union and the States.
Distribution of revenues and the Finance Commission. Revised many times, including by GST in 2016.
Freedom of trade within India and its exceptions.
Civil services and Public Service Commissions.
Tribunals may exist; what is part of the basic structure is the High Courts' and Supreme Court's review over them, not these articles.
Election law-making and the bar on courts during elections.
Reservations in legislatures and services, commissions and lists. Many have sunset clauses or have been amended; upheld when changed.
Linguistic minority protections and the Hindi directive.
Emergency powers. The articles themselves are not part of the basic structure.
Transitional provisions continuing earlier laws, courts and officers.
The right to property. Kesavananda Bharati (Khanna J) held it is not part of the basic structure.
Temporary and special provisions for particular States. Several have been changed or abrogated and upheld.
Abolition of titles. An equality measure, but minor; no case suggests it is essential.
Equal justice and free legal aid, the directive most closely tied to effective access to justice.
Concurrent power over GST, added in 2016. A specific fiscal arrangement within federalism.
Interpretation clause for the Part on finance.
Co-operative societies, added in 2011. Detailed regulatory rules.
Salaries of members and rules of procedure and language in Parliament.
Definitions, interpretation, short title, commencement, the Hindi text and repeals.
Lists the States and Union territories. Parliament changes it by ordinary law under Articles 3 and 4.
Salaries and allowances of constitutional office-holders.
Forms of oaths, including the oath to uphold the Constitution.
Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats. Entrenched, but the numbers change by amendment.
Autonomous districts in the North-East; amended many times.
The Union, State and Concurrent Lists as a scheme are the core of federalism. Individual entries are changed often.
Laws shielded from fundamental rights challenges. Removing the shield would not damage the structure.
The anti-defection law, upheld in Kihoto Hollohan. Repealing it would not breach a basic feature.

amend.s: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but cannot use that power to destroy its identity or make the power unlimited.

jr.s: The High Courts and the Supreme Court must be able to test laws and government action against the Constitution.

indep.s: Judges must be appointed and kept in office free of control by the executive.

rol.c: P. Sambamurthy (1986); I.R. Coelho (2007); Raj Narain (1975)
rol.s: Government acts under law, and its decisions can be tested by independent courts.

equality.t: Equality and the essence of fundamental rights
equality.s: The core of Articles 14, 19 and 21, and the essence of each fundamental right, cannot be abrogated.

balance.t: Balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
balance.s: Parts III and IV must be kept in harmony; neither may be made to swallow the other.

democracy.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994)
democracy.s: Government by elected representatives, with an elected head of state.

elections.s: Elections must be free and fair, and their results open to lawful challenge.

secular.c: S.R. Bommai (1994); I.R. Coelho (2007); Balram Singh (2024)
secular.s: The State treats all religions equally and has no religion of its own.

federal.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); S.R. Bommai (1994)
federal.s: Power is divided between the Union and the States, and the States are not mere agents of the Centre.

sop.c: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, Sikri CJ); I.R. Coelho (2007); Presidential Reference on assent to Bills (2025)
sop.s: Legislature, executive and judiciary each keep their own sphere.

supremacy.s: Every organ of the State is bound by the Constitution.

sovereign.c: Listed by the Lok Sabha Secretariat (2008)
sovereign.s: India is a sovereign Union; its unity and integrity are part of the framework.

parl.c: Listed by the Lok Sabha Secretariat (2008)
parl.s: Ministers are drawn from and answerable to an elected legislature.

access.c: Listed by the Lok Sabha Secretariat (2008)
access.s: People must be able to reach a court to enforce their rights.
